difficultyReason: Single-antecedent principle with straightforward application. Correct answer directly satisfies the stated condition (caused harm = warrants apology).
stimulus: A person should offer an apology if and only if that person has caused harm to another. Apologies serve to acknowledge wrongdoing and rebuild trust; offering one without having caused harm undermines their purpose and comes across as insincere.
questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Marcus accidentally stepped on his roommate's glasses during a party. The glasses were broken, and Marcus apologized immediately.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dr. Chen published research that was later found to be flawed, but she did not apologize because the flaws were unintentional.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elena felt bad about her friend's promotion because she had hoped to be promoted herself, so she apologized for not being happy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A store manager apologized to a customer for the long checkout line, even though the understaffing was due to an unexpected employee absence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: James said sorry to his colleague without explaining what he had done wrong, leaving the colleague confused about the apology.

explanations.correct: Marcus caused harm (broke the glasses) and offered an apology. This directly satisfies the principle's condition.
explanations.B: Violates the principle. Dr. Chen caused harm (published flawed research) but did not apologize. The principle requires an apology when harm is caused, regardless of intent.
explanations.C: Partial fit. Elena apologized, but she did not cause harm to her friend. The principle does not call for apologies without harm caused.
explanations.D: Partial fit. An apology was offered, but the manager did not personally cause the harm (the harm resulted from understaffing). The principle requires that the apologizer must have caused the harm.
explanations.E: Outside scope. The principle addresses whether an apology should be offered, not whether it should be explained clearly.

difficultyReason: Single-antecedent principle about eligibility. Correct answer meets the stated criterion (patent is novel = eligible for protection).
stimulus: A patent is eligible for legal protection if and only if the invention is novel—that is, if no identical invention has been previously disclosed. Protecting non-novel inventions would grant unearned monopolies and hinder progress.
questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A biotech company patented a vaccine that used a method previously described in a 2015 journal article. The patent office denied protection.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An engineer invented a new type of solar panel with a design that had never been disclosed before. The company successfully obtained a patent for it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A researcher developed a minor modification of an existing drug and applied for patent protection, which was granted despite the similarity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A software developer patented a program that was novel but violated existing copyright law. The patent was still issued because novelty was met.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An inventor submitted a patent application for a product that had not yet been disclosed but was still rejected because the market did not seem promising.

explanations.correct: The engineer's solar panel design is novel (never disclosed before) and the patent was obtained. This directly satisfies the principle's condition.
explanations.C: Violates the principle. A minor modification of an existing drug is not novel, yet protection was granted. The principle denies protection for non-novel inventions.
explanations.D: Partial fit. The invention is novel, but the principle does not address copyright law. The existence of copyright issues does not override the novelty criterion for patent eligibility.
explanations.E: Partial fit. The invention is novel and unpatented yet was rejected. The principle bases eligibility on novelty alone, not market potential.

difficultyReason: Single-antecedent principle about ethical obligation. Correct answer matches the stated criterion (promise made = must be kept).
stimulus: An employee should keep a promise to a colleague if the promise was made sincerely and without coercion. Breaking such promises undermines workplace trust and damages professional relationships.
questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Grant promised his supervisor he would meet a deadline, but circumstances changed. He broke the promise and did not apologize.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Under pressure from her boss, Lisa promised to take on extra work. Later, she decided not to keep the promise because it was coerced.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Derek sincerely promised his coworker that he would review her report before the meeting. He kept the promise as agreed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A manager promised a bonus if sales exceeded the target, but when they did, the bonus was not paid due to budget cuts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sofia jokingly promised to bring donuts on Friday, and everyone laughed. She did not bring them, and no one was upset.

explanations.correct: Derek made a sincere promise without coercion and kept it. This directly satisfies the principle.
explanations.A: Violates the principle. Grant made a sincere promise and should have kept it regardless of changed circumstances.
explanations.B: Does not conform. Lisa's promise was coerced, so the principle does not require her to keep it. Her breaking it aligns with the principle's exception.
explanations.D: Partial fit. The manager made a sincere promise, but this scenario is about organizational failure to honor it, not the employee's obligation to keep her promise.
explanations.E: Outside scope. A joking promise does not fall under 'sincere promise,' so the principle does not apply.

difficultyReason: Single-antecedent principle about refund eligibility. Correct answer satisfies the stated criterion (defective product = refund warranted).
stimulus: A retailer must offer a refund to a customer if the product is defective at the time of purchase. Customers are entitled to functioning goods in exchange for their money; selling defective items violates this basic commercial obligation.
questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A customer bought a toaster that worked fine initially but stopped working after six months. The customer requested a refund.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A woman purchased a dress that was defective with a broken zipper. She returned it within days and received a full refund.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A man bought a laptop that was missing a key component when delivered. He requested a repair instead of a refund.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A customer bought a phone with a cracked screen that was sold at a discount. She asked for a refund but was denied.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A buyer returned shoes because they were uncomfortable, even though they were not defective. He received a store credit.

explanations.correct: The dress was defective at purchase (broken zipper) and the customer received a refund. This directly satisfies the principle.
explanations.A: Partial fit. The toaster became defective after purchase, not at time of purchase. The principle applies only to defects present when the product is purchased.
explanations.C: Partial fit. The laptop was defective (missing component) at delivery, but the customer requested repair instead. The principle requires a refund option, though a repair might be acceptable.
explanations.D: Violates the principle. The phone was defective (cracked screen) at purchase, so the principle mandates a refund. Denying it violates the principle.
explanations.E: Outside scope. Discomfort is not a defect. The principle addresses only defective products.

difficultyReason: Single-antecedent principle about appropriate disclosure. Correct answer meets the criterion (conflict of interest exists = disclosure required).
stimulus: A professional has an ethical duty to disclose any conflict of interest before engaging in a transaction. Failing to disclose allows personal interests to potentially override the client's interests, which is a breach of professional responsibility.
questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A real estate agent recommended a property to a buyer without mentioning that the agent's spouse owned the property next door.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An accountant stood to benefit financially from a company's accounting decision. She disclosed the conflict of interest before advising the client.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A lawyer represented a client in contract negotiations without revealing that the lawyer's sister worked for the opposing party.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A financial advisor had no financial stake in any investment product recommended and therefore did not disclose anything.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A consultant disclosed a past conflict of interest from a previous client, even though the current engagement involved different parties.

explanations.correct: The accountant had a conflict of interest (financial benefit from the decision) and disclosed it before advising the client. This directly satisfies the principle.
explanations.A: Violates the principle. The agent had a conflict of interest (spouse's proximity benefit) and did not disclose it.
explanations.C: Violates the principle. The lawyer had a conflict of interest (sister's employment with opposing party) and did not disclose it.
explanations.D: Outside scope. The principle addresses situations where a conflict exists. If no conflict exists, disclosure is not required.
explanations.E: Partial fit. The consultant disclosed, but the disclosure is irrelevant to the current engagement since no conflict exists in the current transaction.

difficultyReason: Single-antecedent principle about merit-based advancement. Correct answer satisfies the criterion (demonstrates required competence = should be promoted).
stimulus: An employee should be promoted to a leadership position if and only if that employee has demonstrated the competencies required for the role. Promoting individuals lacking necessary skills leads to poor management, reduced team morale, and organizational inefficiency.
questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A senior engineer who was loyal to the company for 15 years was promoted to project manager, despite lacking any prior management experience.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A manager who had successfully led three projects and demonstrated strong communication and decision-making skills was promoted to senior director.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An employee with excellent technical skills but poor communication was promoted to lead a team because no other candidates were available.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A promising mid-level analyst who had not yet demonstrated leadership skills remained in her current role pending further development.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An employee with all required leadership competencies was denied promotion because the company preferred internal hiring over external candidates.

explanations.correct: The manager demonstrated the required competencies (leadership, communication, decision-making) and was promoted. This directly satisfies the principle.
explanations.A: Violates the principle. The engineer lacked management competencies but was promoted. The principle forbids promotion without demonstrated competence.
explanations.C: Violates the principle. Poor communication is a missing required competency for team leadership. Promoting despite this violates the principle.
explanations.D: Conforms to the principle. The analyst lacks demonstrated leadership skills, so not promoting her aligns with the principle's requirement.
explanations.E: Partial fit. The employee had the competencies but was denied promotion for an external reason (hiring preference), not competence. The principle addresses only competence-based decisions.
